bridge: Builds on L02 shell argument processing and P05 tests. All examples use harmless local text; never execute commands supplied by a request.
teaching:
Command injection happens when data changes command structure. A shell interprets syntax before starting programs, so interpolating untrusted text into a shell command expands the attack surface. An argument-vector API can avoid shell parsing, but the invoked program may still interpret options or special input.

Prefer an in-process library when it can perform the task. If a subprocess is needed, fix the executable, pass separate arguments, validate the requested operation and enforce time/resource limits. shell=False is an important boundary, not proof that every argument is safe for every tool.

Test both ordinary data and option-like input. Consider filenames beginning with a dash, working-directory assumptions and inherited environment variables. The security question is which interpreter receives the data and what syntax it recognises at that stage.

In the shell demonstration, & is a single ampersand: in a shell such as Bash it starts an asynchronous command. The two-character operator && means run the next command only if the previous one succeeded. These are different operations. Percent encoding belongs to the HTTP-form transport layer; shell quoting and parsing happen later. Avoid treating a string that is safe at one layer as safe for every later interpreter.
explanation: The public input is a document key rather than a command or arbitrary filename. Reading uses a language library, so shell grammar is never involved. This also simplifies expected outputs and error handling.
exercise: Run the example with greeting and an unknown key. On paper compare subprocess.run(["fixed-tool", user_value], shell=False) with constructing one shell command string. Identify a remaining argument/option risk in the first design.
solution: greeting returns hello; unknown keys raise the explicit error. An argument vector avoids shell tokenisation, but a value like an option can still be interpreted by the selected executable. Validate the tool's own argument grammar.
challenge: Paper design only: an image-conversion endpoint supports mode thumbnail or grayscale. Map thumbnail to the fixed argument list ["--size", "128x128"] and grayscale to ["--grayscale"] for a fictional fixed executable. Evaluate thumbnail, grayscale, unknown and --delete-all. Show why the caller’s raw mode string never becomes a shell command or raw tool flag. Do not run the fictional tool.
challenge_solution: Use a dictionary whose keys are thumbnail and grayscale and whose values are those fixed lists. Look up the mode; reject if absent. Both named modes select only their predefined arguments; unknown and --delete-all are rejected before starting anything. If the real design needs a process, pass a fixed executable and the selected arguments through an argument-vector API, with separate controlled input/output paths and limits. This paper map removes raw flag selection; tool-specific file handling and permissions still need review.
